summary: Atlantic Canada's first national park, across the northern tip of Cape Breton Island between the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Atlantic. A forested plateau breaks off in sea cliffs and deep river canyons, and 106 kilometres of the Cabot Trail climb over it. Most visitors come to drive the trail, walk the Skyline headland above the Gulf and watch for moose, bald eagles and whales.
story: The Cape Breton Plateau is a worn-down remnant of the Appalachian chain that runs from Georgia to Newfoundland. Its rolling top averages about 400 metres, rising above 500 at the centre, and some of the oldest rocks in the Maritime provinces lie in the Blair River inlier at its northern end. Faults, glaciers and rivers have cut the plateau into steep-walled canyons. On the west it meets the Gulf of St. Lawrence in cliffs; on the east it slopes more gently to the Atlantic, with low headlands and a few long sandy beaches.

The cool maritime climate and the height of the plateau bring together Acadian, boreal and taiga habitats, a mix Parks Canada says is found nowhere else in Canada. Boreal forest covers most of the uplands and Acadian forest the lowlands; in the Grande Anse Valley sugar maples 350 years old form one of the largest old-growth hardwood forests in the Maritimes. Forty species of land mammal live here, among them moose, black bear, coyote and snowshoe hare, alongside Bicknell's thrush, Atlantic salmon and small populations of arctic-alpine plants left by the last ice age. Woodland caribou disappeared in the 1920s; 51 brought from Québec in 1968 and 1969 were last seen in 1972.

The park lies in Unama'ki, a district of Mi'kma'ki, the unceded territory of the Mi'kmaq, who helped successive waves of Acadian, Scottish, Irish and other settlers adapt to the island. Remains of their settlements survive along the coast: at La Bloc more than thirty French families once fished and ran a cannery, and at Fishing Cove Scottish settlers fished the Gulf and traded with the French.

After long lobbying by Nova Scotia, northern Cape Breton was chosen for a national park in 1936, the first in Atlantic Canada and still the largest in the Maritimes. Families were expropriated to make it, a practice Parks Canada ended in the 1970s; since 2011 their descendants can claim free admission. In 2025 the Mi'kmaq of Nova Scotia and Parks Canada signed the Toqi'maliaptmu'k Arrangement — 'we will look after it together' — to co-manage the province's Parks Canada places, this park among them.
howItWorks: A park pass is required to drive the Cabot Trail through the park and to use its campgrounds, trails and other facilities, including the Highlands Links golf course. Daily admission is $10.00 for an adult, as listed in November 2026; youth 17 and under enter free. The national Discovery Pass — $83.50 adult, $71.50 senior, $167.50 for a family or group of up to seven people arriving in one vehicle, as listed in November 2026 — covers admission here and at more than 80 Parks Canada places for 12 months. The Canada Strong Pass gave free admission from 19 June to 7 September 2026; regular fees resumed on 8 September 2026. The Mi'kmaq of Nova Scotia enter without charge with a vehicle identifier from their band office, and families expropriated for the park can apply for a free admission pass.

Campsites at Chéticamp, Mkwesaqtuk/Cap-Rouge, Ingonish Beach, Broad Cove and the Fishing Cove backcountry campground are booked through the Parks Canada Reservation Service, online at reservation.pc.gc.ca or on 1-877-737-3783; reservations for 2027 open on Wednesday 10 February 2027 at 8 am Atlantic time. Corney Brook, MacIntosh Brook and Big Intervale are first come, first served. From 26 June to 25 October 2026 the Skyline Trail could be reached only with a timed parking reservation booked through the same service; check before you go whether reservations apply on your dates.

Fishing Cove is the only designated wilderness campsite. Campers must register for a backcountry permit at the Chéticamp or Ingonish visitor centre, cook on a stove and pack out all garbage; to camp anywhere else in the backcountry you must ask the park wardens, the only staff who can issue that permit. Fishing needs a national park fishing permit and a park pass; provincial licences are not valid inside the park. Keep at least 30 metres from all wildlife and never feed it.

sights.name: Skyline Trail
sights.note: From the top of French Mountain a level path crosses the plateau to a boardwalk on a headland cliff high above the Gulf: 6.5 km out and back or an 8.2 km loop. Watch for moose and whales.

sights.name: Fishing Cove
sights.note: A 6 km descent from 355 metres to a grassy cove and cobble beach, once a Scottish fishing settlement and now the park's only wilderness campsite.

sights.name: Lone Shieling
sights.note: A replica Scottish crofter's hut at the start of a short loop through 350-year-old sugar maples in the Grande Anse Valley, one of the park's most protected areas.

sights.name: Beulach Ban Falls
sights.note: A 21-metre cascade 50 metres from the Aspy trailhead, at the end of a side road off the Cabot Trail. The Aspy trail follows the Aspy fault from here.

sights.name: Mary Ann Falls
sights.note: A cascade popular for swimming, reached by a trail along an old alignment of the Cabot Trail on the eastern side of the park.

sights.name: Franey
sights.note: A climb from near sea level to 423 metres, where a lookout faces the Clyburn Brook canyon and the Atlantic coast from Cape Smokey to Ingonish. A 4.5 km lower loop or 13 km full loop.

sights.name: Middle Head
sights.note: A 5.3 km trail out to headland cliffs at Ingonish, overlooking the Atlantic, Cape Smokey and Ingonish Island.

sights.name: Chéticamp Visitor Centre
sights.note: The western entrance: exhibits on the park, passes and programme tickets, and Le Nique nature bookshop. The Acadian Trail climbs 365 metres from across the road. Mid-May to late October.

sights.name: Ingonish Visitor Centre
sights.note: The eastern entrance, opened in 2014, beside Freshwater Lake. Passes, programme tickets and park information. Mid-May to late October.

entrances: Chéticamp, on the west side — reached by Route 19 (the Ceilidh Trail) from the Canso Causeway or by the Cabot Trail through the Margaree valley
Ingonish Beach, on the east side — reached by the Cabot Trail through St. Ann's or by the short Englishtown ferry
The Cabot Trail itself, which runs for 106 km through the park and is open year-round
planYourVisit.reservations: Frontcountry campsites at Chéticamp, Mkwesaqtuk/Cap-Rouge, Ingonish Beach and Broad Cove, the Fishing Cove backcountry sites and guided hikes are booked through the Parks Canada Reservation Service; 2027 bookings open on 10 February 2027 at 8 am Atlantic time. In the 2026 peak season the Skyline Trail needed a timed parking reservation from 26 June to 25 October, with no access once all slots were taken. Check with Parks Canada before you go.
permits: A park pass for the Cabot Trail and all park facilities
A backcountry permit for Fishing Cove, from the Chéticamp or Ingonish visitor centre; wardens issue permits for camping anywhere else
A national park fishing permit (and a salmon angling permit for the Chéticamp River)
A Skyline Trail parking reservation in peak season
camping: Reservable campgrounds at Chéticamp, Mkwesaqtuk/Cap-Rouge, Ingonish Beach and Broad Cove, with oTENTiks and tiny cabins
First-come campgrounds at Corney Brook, MacIntosh Brook and Big Intervale
Fishing Cove backcountry campground, eight sites, stove only
Camping season 15 May to 26 October in 2026
lodging: Accommodation in the communities along the Cabot Trail outside the park, among them Chéticamp and Ingonish
The Keltic Lodge property at Ingonish Beach is leased to a private operator; its main lodge has been closed since April 2024
seasonalClosures: Visitor centres and most services run from mid-May to 25 October; full services only in July and August — check with Parks Canada before you go
The Cabot Trail stays open all winter, but services in the park are limited

weather: Northern Cape Breton has warm summers, cold winters and weather that changes fast between the Gulf and the Atlantic. The plateau, at about 400 metres, has its own colder climate, with a shorter growing season and more precipitation than the coast; 300 to 400 centimetres of snow fall each year, and drifts linger in the highlands into June. Fog is common. In autumn tropical storms can bring torrential rain, and on the west coast south-easterly winds known locally as les suetes can gust to 200 km/h as they pour off the plateau. July and August are the busy months; late September and October bring the autumn colours.
directions: The park is about a two-hour drive from the Canso Causeway, two hours from Sydney and five hours from Halifax. The Cabot Trail loops for nearly 300 kilometres round northern Cape Breton. For the western entrance at Chéticamp, take Route 19 from Port Hastings through Mabou and Inverness, or the Cabot Trail from exit 7 of Highway 105 at Nyanza. For the eastern entrance at Ingonish, take the Cabot Trail from exit 11 at South Haven, or Route 312 from exit 12, which includes a five-minute ferry at Englishtown. Electric vehicle chargers are spread through the park at six locations.

fees.title: Daily admission
fees.detail: Adult. Senior $8.75; family or group $19.50; youth free. A seasonal pass costs $48.25 for an adult. As listed by Parks Canada in November 2026; check before you go.

fees.title: Parks Canada Discovery Pass
fees.detail: Adult, 12 months at more than 80 Parks Canada places. Senior $71.50; family or group $167.50. As listed by Parks Canada in November 2026; check before you go.

fees.title: Skyline Trail parking
fees.detail: Per vehicle per day with a reservation, plus a $3.50 online reservation fee, on top of admission. As listed by Parks Canada in November 2026; check before you go.

fees.title: Backcountry camping
fees.detail: Per person per night at Fishing Cove. As listed by Parks Canada in November 2026; check before you go.

fees.title: National park fishing permit

chronology.text: Cape Breton Highlands National Park is created, the first national park in Atlantic Canada.
The Cabot Trail is realigned near Mary Ann Falls; the old road later becomes the trail to the falls.
Fifty-one woodland caribou from Québec are released in the park; the last is seen in 1972.
Parks Canada ends the practice of expropriating land for parks.
The Admission Pass for Expropriated Families is introduced.
The new Ingonish visitor centre opens.
A new management plan is tabled, prepared with the Mi'kmaq of Nova Scotia.
The Keltic main lodge closes in April for advanced deterioration.
The Mi'kmaq of Nova Scotia and Parks Canada sign the Toqi'maliaptmu'k co-management Arrangement.
Timed parking reservations are introduced at the Skyline Trail from 26 June to 25 October.

safety: Black bears, coyotes and moose live throughout the park. Keep 30 metres away, hike in company with a solid stick, consider carrying bear spray, and keep children close. Cow moose are most dangerous from mid-May to the end of June, bulls from mid-September.
Moose often stand on the Cabot Trail and are hard to see at dusk. Drive within the speed limit and avoid driving after dark.
Stay on the Skyline boardwalk. Off-trail paths lead to unstable cliff edges, and the narrow headland has only one way out if you meet a moose or bear.
Weather on the plateau and coast changes quickly. Carry water and layers, tell someone your route, and expect black flies and mosquitoes all summer.
regulations: A park pass is required on the Cabot Trail within the park and for all facilities.
Never approach or feed wildlife, even indirectly by leaving food or litter; keep dogs on a leash.
Fish only with a national park fishing permit, single barbless hooks and no lead; scheduled waters are fly fishing only, and all Atlantic salmon must be released.
Camp only in designated campgrounds; backcountry camping needs a permit, and Fishing Cove allows stoves only, no open fires.
